summary: Find files by name, type or age
Run a command on each file find finds
description: -exec, -execdir, -ok and -okdir run a command of their arguments' choosing.

summary: Write what find finds to a file
description: -fprint, -fprint0, -fprintf and -fls write to the file they name.

summary: Search files or input for a pattern
Search every file below a directory
description: A recursive search reads everything under a directory, secrets included, by names no argument spells: -r, -R, --recursive, --dereference-recursive, and -d or --directories recurse, which grep takes abbreviated as far as rec. The word after -d is held only in those spellings, so a file or a pattern that starts rec, records.log, stays a read; -drecurse is an option with an r in it, and --directories=rec is caught by what follows its =.
file -C, or --compile, which file takes abbreviated, writes a .mgc file.

summary: Guess the types of files named in a file, or by a magic file
description: file -f, or --files-from, names each line of the file it reads, and -m, or --magic-file, quotes a magic file's lines it cannot read: either prints a file of its argument's choosing, by a name the secret globs do not see when it is written onto the option, -f.kube/config. Every option with an f or an m in it is held to this, --mime-type and --dereference too, since file takes short options together and long ones abbreviated.

summary: Print a file, or its start or end
Page through a file, running a pager command first
description: less runs a + argument as a command when it starts: less '+!cmd' runs cmd.

summary: Page through a file, logging it or with key bindings of its own
description: -o and -O, --log-file and --LOG-FILE, write the input to a file; -k and --lesskey-* bind keys, shell escapes among them.
diff only with -q or --brief first, which say whether files differ and never what is in them, whatever follows: cmp of a directory fails.

diff of two directories, with no -r, prints every file they share by name that differs, secrets included, by names no argument spells -- diff /proc/1 /proc/2 prints both environments -- and a directory is not told from a file by its name: so every diff that prints contents is held to this, as grep -r is.

A recursive diff, -r or --recursive, prints files that differ under two directories, and -N, --new-file or --unidirectional-new-file prints a file missing from the other whole: either reads files, secrets included, by names no argument spells, as grep -r does. Every option with an r in it is held to this, since diff takes long ones abbreviated.

summary: Cut, translate or reverse lines of text
description: uniq only bare or with one of these: a second file argument is a file it writes.
-o and --output write a file; every option with an o in it is held to this, since sort takes long ones abbreviated.

summary: Sort the files another file names
description: --files0-from, taken as abbreviated as --fil, sorts and prints every file named in the file it names, which no argument spells and so no secret path catches, as grep -r is held to a write. --files0-from spelt in full has an o in it, and is held to sort-output too.

summary: Sort through a program of its arguments' choosing
description: --compress-program runs the program it names on sort's temporary files, taken as abbreviated as --co; an --output too, which is held to the stricter of the two.

summary: Say which program a command name runs
description: Not command -v or -V: frisket reads command only as running the command after it, and any option of it as unreadable, since csh has no such builtin and runs whatever program is named command.
mount only bare or with -l: with anything else it mounts.

summary: List the filesystems a file names
description: findmnt -F, or --tab-file, prints the file it reads as a table of filesystems, and a line of three words is one, by a name the secret globs do not see when it is written onto the option, -F.kube/config.

summary: Show how long the machine has been up
Show the kernel and machine name
description: hostname only in these forms: given a name, or -F, it sets the machine's.

summary: Show the host's name, clock and locale settings
List the hardware and loaded kernel modules
Look PCI devices up over DNS, or in files of the argument's choosing
description: lspci -q, -qq and -Q look IDs up over DNS and write what they learn to a cache, and -O sets where: -O net.domain=<domain> queries a domain of its choosing, -O net.cache_name=<file> replaces the file, and -O dump.name, -F, -i and -p read a file of its choosing as a dump, an ID database or a module map. lspci takes short options together, so every option with one of these letters in it is held to this.

-H and -A pick an access method, direct hardware access among them, -M probes every bus, and -xxx and -xxxx read config space that some devices fail on being read: as root, each can hang the machine. lspci counts its -x however they are written, -x -x -x and -xx -x as much as -xxx, so every option with an x in it is held to this, -x and -xx too.

date -f, or --file, prints every line of the file it reads that is no date, so it prints the file, by a name the secret globs do not see when it is written onto the option, -f.kube/config. Every option with an f in it is held to this, --rfc-3339 and --reference too, since date takes short options together and long ones abbreviated.
date -s or --set sets the clock, and so does an argument of digits, MMDDhhmm: every argument starting with a digit is held to this, -d 10:00's too.
ps only in these forms: its BSD e shows each process's environment, as does -o's environ column, which process-environment refuses.
ps -o environ prints each process's environment: the login user's processes', or every one's as root. Held to it in any word that holds it, as a list's pid,environ, environ= and environ:40 do.

summary: List the sockets to a host, which looks it up
description: lsof -i @<host>, and -iTCP@<host>:<port>, look the host up: the machine's resolver asks DNS for a name of the argument's choosing, and so carries what is written into it off the machine. Every word with an @ in it is held to this.

summary: Show who is logged in, and who you are
Read a login log of the argument's choosing
description: last -f, or --file, prints the file it reads as login records, by a name the secret globs do not see when it is written onto the option, -f.kube/config. Every option with an f in it is held to this, --fulltimes and --time-format too, since last takes long ones abbreviated.

systemctl show with no unit shows the service manager's own properties, its environment among them, which read-environment refuses in the usual spellings, and service-manager-environment wherever a word names it.

summary: Run systemctl on a disk image or a directory tree
description: --image mounts a disk image of the argument's choosing, as journalctl's does, and --root reads units from a tree of its choosing; each as systemctl takes it abbreviated, --image-policy too.

-H and --host reach another machine over SSH; -M and --machine a container's or another user's service manager, and -C and --capsule a capsule's, whose units' files systemctl cat prints. A --property= naming a property with an M, an H or a C in it is refused with them: give it to -p as a word of its own, -p MainPID.

summary: Reboot, shut down or suspend the machine
description: systemctl exit asks the system manager to exit, which outside a container powers the machine off, and default isolates default.target.

summary: Reboot, shut down or suspend the machine by starting its target
description: systemctl start reboot.target, or its systemd-reboot.service, is systemctl reboot, exit.target outside a container is poweroff.target, and factory-reset.target resets the machine at its next boot and reboots it: these units are held to power whatever the verb, so systemctl status reboot.target is too.

summary: Rotate, vacuum, flush or sync the journal, or mount an image to read
description: Each as journalctl takes it abbreviated: --rotate, --vacuum-*, --flush, --sync and --synchronize-on-exit, --relinquish-var, --smart-relinquish-var, --setup-keys, --update-catalog; --cursor-file, which writes the file it reads; and --image, which mounts one.

summary: Clear the kernel's log, or change what reaches the console
description: -c, -C, -D, -E and -n, and the long options they are; every option with one of those letters in it is held to this, since dmesg takes long ones abbreviated.

summary: Read a kernel log of the argument's choosing
description: dmesg -F, or --file, and -K, or --kmsg-file, print the file they read as the kernel's log, by a name the secret globs do not see when it is written onto the option, -F.kube/config.

summary: Show addresses, links, routes and neighbours
description: ip only in these forms: it takes every verb abbreviated, so ip a a adds an address, and -b runs a file of commands.

summary: List installed packages and their files
description: dpkg only in these forms, since it does everything else too; dpkg-query only reads.
--pre-invoke and --post-invoke run a command by sh -c.

summary: Set apt's configuration on the command line
description: -o and -c, --option and --config-file, set any of apt's configuration, its hooks and paths among them: every option with an o or a c in it is held to this, --no-install-recommends too, since apt takes short options together.

summary: Have apt-cache rebuild its cache into a file of the argument's choosing
description: -p and -s, --pkg-cache and --src-cache, name the cache files, and apt-cache rebuilds one that is not a cache and renames it over the file: apt-cache policy -p /home/ops/.profile replaces .profile. apt takes them too for the verbs it hands to apt-cache: search, policy, depends, rdepends and showsrc, but not list or show. Every option with a p or an s in it is held to this, --names-only and --installed too, since apt takes short options together.

summary: Install a package from a file
description: A package file's scripts run as root, and its file is whatever was written there.

summary: Remove containers, images, volumes or networks
Create files, or change their times
Change files' owners, modes or attributes
Write disks, filesystems or partitions directly
Read a disk or partition raw
description: A filesystem read raw is every file in it, /etc/shadow and every key, by no name of theirs, as dd of it is. Only these commands, which print what they read -- date -f, dmesg -F, last -f, and who and users of a file, print it as dates, a log or logins: lsblk, df and findmnt name a device to say what it is. A device is caught by its own name in a path of any spelling only for the common disks' names; a glob with a / in it matches the word whole, so /dev/sde1, /dev/root, and anything below /dev -- /dev/block/8:1, LVM's /dev/ubuntu-vg/ubuntu-lv -- are caught spelt from /dev, but not from a cd into it. /dev/null, /dev/zero, /dev/stdin and the like are not disks, and stay reads.

summary: Add, change or remove users and groups, or their passwords
Read a private key or keystore
description: key.txt and keys.txt are age's identities, where sops keeps them: ~/.config/sops/age/keys.txt, /var/lib/sops-nix/key.txt.

summary: Read password hashes or saved passwords
description: *password* is a file named for one, sops-nix's dan-password as much as a database's, and a search for the word, grep password, as *token* is: shadow holds the hashes, and passwd names no secret.

A token or a password is as often an environment variable as a file: env with no command, and with options that run none, printenv, either by its usual paths, the shells' set, export -p, declare -p and typeset, zsh's local, csh's setenv, and the service manager's environment, which systemctl show with no unit prints among its properties, print them all. systemctl show with other options and no unit is a read all the same: give it a unit, or -p for what it is.

show-environment wherever it is among systemctl's words, as systemctl --user show-environment has it, and every property named for the environment, -p Environment and --property=Environment, the manager's or a unit's, which hold what was imported into them.

summary: Read environment files or a process's environment
Read a secrets directory, a token or a keyring
description: secrets* is a secrets directory however it is named, sops-nix's /run/secrets.d/<generation> and /run/secrets-for-users.d among them, which /run/secrets only links to; sops* and agenix* their keys and what they decrypt into; keys NixOS's /run/keys; credstore* systemd's credentials.

summary: Read a shell's or a client's history

description: /dev/mem and a process's /proc/<pid>/mem are spelt from / so that a search for the word, grep mem /proc/meminfo, is not refused; read after cd /dev or cd /proc/1 by a name of its own, mem is not, as a disk is not.
